Day 1. Over tea, Lalit tells Vijay, "Twenty-five kids in a room and I can hold every one of them. Sales is just talking." The company's product-training video stays unwatched.

Day 9. The target sheet says forty calls a day. Lalit's first cold call ends in a click after eight seconds. So does the second. Explaining everything patiently, the way it works in a classroom, gets nowhere when the listener can simply hang up. By evening Lalit has booked no visits at all.

Day 21. Lalit is far behind on targets. Vijay says, "You never asked what the job needed." Lalit opens a notebook and writes two columns: what I assumed, and what actually happened. The second column is much longer.

qa.q: How many calls a day did the target sheet require?
qa.a: The target sheet said forty calls a day.

qa.q: What was Lalit feeling after the first cold call ended in a click?
qa.a: Lalit felt surprised and rattled, because the confidence from the classroom did not work on a stranger who could hang up.

qa.q: What could Lalit have done before the first day to test the assumption?
qa.a: Lalit could have listened in on a senior's calls or practised a few mock cold calls, so the gaps showed up early instead of against targets.

qa.q: How might Vijay see Lalit's plan?
qa.a: Vijay may see it as confident but untested, and may feel concerned watching Lalit skip the training video and then fall behind.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher moving into sales who assumes classroom skills will transfer and is caught out by targets and cold-calling.

passage:
"Himani, you're sure your coaching experience will carry you in sales? Let me tell you what happened to me, your Lavanya aunty, at twenty-two.
I'd taught maths at a school for a year. Explaining, persuading children, handling parents, I thought, is that not sales? So I joined a company selling educational software. I didn't ask anyone what the job really was.
The first week, they gave me a list of two hundred schools and a phone. Cold calls. People hung up on me before I'd finished my name. And every Monday there was a target on the whiteboard, and my name at the bottom.
In a classroom, children have to listen. On a phone, nobody has to. I hadn't known that. I'd never checked.
I lasted five months. If I had spent one day shadowing a salesperson first, I'd have known what to prepare for."

qa.q: How many schools were on Lavanya's first calling list?
qa.a: There were two hundred schools on the list.

qa.q: How did young Lavanya feel in the first weeks of the sales job?
qa.a: She felt surprised and discouraged, with people hanging up on her and her name at the bottom of the target board.

qa.q: What was the key choice in Lavanya's story, and what could have changed it?
qa.a: Joining without asking what the job really involved was the key choice; spending a day shadowing a salesperson would have shown the gaps.

qa.q: How might the school principals Lavanya called have seen her calls?
qa.a: They probably saw just another unknown sales call during a busy day, which is why they hung up before she finished her name.

grounding: Shows a teacher moving into sales assuming classroom skills would be enough and being surprised by cold calls and targets.

Dilnaz left her school teaching job on a Friday and started at an insurance company's sales team on Monday, in the middle of the monsoon, with a two-hour commute across flooded roads.
"You'll be great," she had told herself. "I talk to thirty children a day. I explain things. I handle angry parents."
Gurpreet, her team lead, handed her a headset and a list. "Forty calls today. Target this month is twelve policies."
By lunch Dilnaz had made twenty-two calls. Nineteen people hung up. Two said they'd think about it. One shouted. She realised no one had to listen to her; in class, everyone did.
The target board by the pantry showed her name with a zero. At six she stood at a bus stop in ankle-deep water, wondering why she had never asked anyone in sales what an ordinary day was like before she resigned.

qa.q: How many calls had Dilnaz made by lunch?
What was Dilnaz feeling at the flooded bus stop?
qa.a: She felt shaken and doubtful, wondering why she never asked what an ordinary sales day was like before resigning.

qa.q: What approach would have suited Dilnaz better before switching?
qa.a: Talking to people in sales or trying a few calls beforehand would have tested her assumption that teaching skills were enough.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet see Dilnaz's first day?
qa.a: Gurpreet may see a new person who is surprised by the pace, and may know from experience that teachers often expect sales to feel like class.

grounding: Shows a teacher moving into sales who assumed classroom experience would be enough and is surprised by targets and cold calling.
